title: In 74 held-out OpenNeuro fMRI studies (TR ≤ 1 s), the slow global BOLD signal has the same regional lag order in every study, cerebellum about 1 s last; tasks keep most of the order with smaller lags
abstract:
In fast fMRI from 74 held-out public studies, the slow brain-wide BOLD signal reaches the brain regions in the same time order in every study; task runs keep most of this order, change it somewhat, and make the delays smaller. This order is mostly the known delay map of the global (systemic and arousal-related) BOLD fluctuation; because it is the same across studies, scanners and tasks, lagged-connectivity results must be checked against it, and tasks mainly change the size of the delays rather than reversing their order.

Data: ReadyNeuro (minimally preprocessed OpenNeuro fMRI; no slice-timing correction, no nuisance regression), runs with a repetition time (TR) of 1 s or less, 71 regions. The lag projection of a region is its mean time delay relative to all other regions, from the 0.01-0.1 Hz cross-covariance (positive = later); without global-signal regression (GSR) it is nearly the same as the delay relative to the global signal (median r = 0.95). A template from 15 discovery studies (20 people) was frozen and nine tests were pre-registered on held-out data: 31 studies with rest runs (48 people) and 43 task-only studies (52 people). All nine passed; one (a dorsal-attention shift in task) only weakly.

Each held-out rest map correlated with the template (median r = 0.65, 31 of 31 studies; pooled map r = 0.95; with GSR r = 0.26). Putamen, amygdala, somatomotor and dorsal-attention cortex came first; cerebellum and brainstem came a median 0.96 s after cortex in 31 of 31 studies. Task maps kept the order (median r = 0.48, 20 of 20 studies; 0.59 in 43 of 43 task-only studies; 98 distinct task labels across the held-out sets); time-reversed task runs gave r = -0.48. The lag pattern was smaller in task: ratio 0.73 with the pre-registered rest template (p < 0.001), 0.88 by the template-free map SD (p = 0.016), 0.92 by split-half covariance (p = 0.053); not significant with GSR. Task maps also fit the rest template less well than rest maps. Correlational checks did not link it to motion (DVARS) or global-signal amplitude. An arterial transit time template matched part of the cortical order (median r = 0.31) but shows no cerebellar delay. New is the scale and the many-task test; a largely vascular lag map, its persistence in one task and a late cerebellum were known from single cohorts. Limits: 1-3 people per study, coarse regions after rigid alignment, no physiological recordings, partial volume and slice timing not corrected, run order not controlled.

display.caption: Rest lag order. A: lag projection of the 71 regions (dots) by network, held-out confirmation studies pooled, without (blue) and with (orange) global-signal regression; bars are network means. B: pooled confirmation map against the frozen discovery template (r = 0.95). C: per-study correlation with the template (discovery: leave-one-study-out; confirmation: frozen template); bars are medians.

Rest versus task (raw signals). A: correlation of study maps with the rest template for rest maps, task maps of the same studies, task maps of task-only studies, and the time-reversed control. B: rest-half versus task-half correlation against the within-condition split-half correlation (noise ceiling); crosses are the time-reversed control. C: amplitude of the rest template in the task map versus the rest map, per study (dashed line = no change); template-free measures give a smaller reduction (files/figures/fig4_compression_measures.png). D: dorsal attention network shift (task minus rest) without and with global-signal regression, and after injecting a 0.5 s delay into the task runs.

Raw rest lag projection (confirmation pool) against arterial transit time from the BATS ASL template. A: 52 cortical regions. B: subcortical structures, brainstem and cerebellum (orange: subcortex; green: brainstem and cerebellum); the square is the cortical mean.
